text.p: These are the key facts about Indonesia:
POPULATION: 200 million, making it the world's fourth most populous country after China, India and the United States. About 120 million people live on Java island.

Islam is the main religion, accounting for 87 percent of the population in Indonesia, which has more than 300 ethnic groups. Roman Catholics, Protestants, Buddhists, Hindus and Animists make up most of the rest. Bahasa Indonesia, similar to Malay, is the official language.

AREA: 1,919,270 sq km (741,000 sq miles) spread over 17,508 islands, of which only 6,000 are inhabited. Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines lie to the north, Papua New Guinea to the east and Australia to the south and southeast.
CAPITAL: Jakarta (population more than 10 million)

ARMED FORCES: (Military Balance of International Institute for Strategic Studies) Total est. 299,200 personnel, with reserves of about 400,000. Internal opposition includes Fretilin (Revolutionary Force for an Independent East Timor), the Free Papua Movement (OPM) and the Free Aceh Movement (Gerakan Aceh Merdeka)
Army 235,200 personnel, nearly 1,000 light tanks and mechanised infantry combat vehicles.

Navy 43,000-strong, including 12,000 marines and 1,000 naval air. Two submarines, 17 frigates, some with Exocet missiles, 57 patrol and coastal warships, 35 patrol craft, 13 minesweepers and 28 amphibious and 15 support craft.
Air force 21,000 men, 77 combat aircraft, including U.S.-designed F-16s and British Hawks, but no armed helicopters.
The 174,000-strong police force is under the command of the armed forces.
ECONOMY: Annual per capita income $1,000. GDP (1996 estimate) $209 billion.

MAIN EXPORTS: Indonesia is Asia's only member of OPEC and an important crude oil source for Japan. It is the world's biggest exporter of liquefied natural gas. Timber and timber products are major exports and it is the world's largest plywood exporter.

Indonesia is also the world's second largest exporter of rubber and palm oil and third largest exporter of coffee and cocoa. Other key exports are tea, tin and textiles. Oil and gas provide around 30 percent of export earnings, down from 80 percent in the early 1980s.
Its trade surplus rose to $5.3 billion in the 1996 January- October period from $3.1 billion in the same 1995 period.

The 1997/98 (April-March) budget, balanced by law, was projected to rise 11.6 percent from 1996/97 to 101.09 trillion rupiah ($42.8 billion). The 1997/98 current account deficit was expected to be $9.798 billion, compared to an estimated $8.823 billion in 1996/97.

Indonesia, with a history of prompt servicing of a foreign debt now more than $100 billion (including $54.6 billion in government foreign debt as of November 30, 1996), accepts sizeable aid each year from the World Bank and Western donors.
The Consultative Group on Indonesia, a group of nations and multilateral agencies giving aid to Indonesia, pledged to provide $5.26 billion in aid in 1996 against $5.36 billion in 1995.
The debt-service ratio was expected to be 31.2 percent in fiscal 1997/98 compared with an estimated 31.7 percent in 1996/97.

Since the late 1980s, the government has initiated a series of economic deregulations to open up the banking sector and fire up the Jakarta stock market. It approved $29.9 billion in foreign investment in 1996 against $39.9 billion in 1995.
The government projected inflation in the 1997 calendar year at six percent, compared with 6.47 in 1996 and 8.64 percent in 1995.
It projected economic growth of between 7.6 and 7.9 percent for the 1997/98 fiscal year, compared with around 8.2 percent in 1996/97.

HISTORY: Indonesia declared independence in 1945 after an almost uninterrupted 350 years under Dutch rule. During the Napoleonic wars, when the Netherlands was occupied by France, the French laid claim to Dutch possessions overseas. The British intervened in Indonesia, seizing control from combined French- Dutch forces to rule from 1811-16. By treaty, the Dutch returned to power after Napoleon's defeat.

By the early 20th century, attempts to overthrow the Dutch by force were replaced by the development of nationalist organisations, which sought change and reform through political means. The Japanese invasion in 1942 and occupation until 1945 strengthened the determination of nationalist forces.

The country's fiery first president, Sukarno, was replaced in 1967 by Suharto, then an army general, following what the government said was a Communist-inspired plot attempt at the end of September 1965.
Political analysts say up to 500,000 people died, primarily in communal violence, between October 1965 and early 1966.
The government and military stress the need for stability in the sprawling archipelago of disparate people, and have on occasion in the past enforced this with a heavy hand.

In December 1975, Indonesian troops invaded the former Portuguese colony of East Timor with tacit Western consent, and incorporated the territory as the country's 27th province the following July. The United Nations has refused to recognise the move, which continues to bedevil Indonesia's foreign image two decades later.
Suharto (born June 8, 1921) was re-elected unopposed for a sixth five-year term in March 1993, and is widely expected to seek office again in 1998 following the general elections in May 1997.

While an authoritarian leader who has followed the precept of divide-and-rule with success against potential political opponents, Suharto is widely credited with promoting Indonesia's economic growth. The big challenge now faced by the government is to ensure the wealth percolates down through society and to the poorer eastern areas of the country.

In constitutional theory, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), a 1,000-member group dominated by political appointees, is the highest state organ. It meets once every five years to elect a president and set policy guidelines. The president, his Golkar party and the military are the dominant political forces.

Indonesia is a member of of the 111-member Non-Aligned Movement, the Conference of the Islamic Organisation and the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. It is the biggest member of the seven-nation Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN), which has its secretariat in Jakarta.
